## Vocabulary

- **self**: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring (12/8)

## How it works

- [statement] An Ethereum reorg can cause OP Stack nodes to downgrade safe transactions to unsafe while the sequencer republishes their data. Treat commitment status as capable of regression before finalization. (low confidence) — https://docs.optimism.io/stack/transactions/transaction-finality · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Using a finalized Solana blockhash reduces dropped-fork risk but consumes more of the transaction expiry window because that blockhash is older. Waiting for finality after submission and selecting the signing blockhash are separate monitor concerns. (high confidence) — https://solana.com/developers/cookbook/transactions/confirmation · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring · also: https://www.helius.dev/blog/solana-commitment-levels
- [statement] Envio database rollback does not undo handler API calls, external caches, or external files. For a bot monitor, reconciliation of indexed chain state therefore cannot be assumed to reverse an external action already triggered by that state. (low confidence) — https://docs.envio.dev/docs/HyperIndex/reorgs-support · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] On standard OP Stack rollups, unsafe, safe and finalized identify distinct trust stages: sequencer inclusion, publication on Ethereum, and finalization of the Ethereum block containing the data. A monitor should record the actual stage rather than label every sequencer inclusion final. (low confidence) — https://docs.optimism.io/stack/transactions/transaction-finality · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring
- [statement] A fixed delay behind the chain tip reduces reorg exposure but does not guarantee immunity. Trail of Bits recommends choosing probabilistic-finality delays using historical reorg behavior and economic attack cost, rather than treating a universal confirmation count as finality. (high confidence) — https://www.quicknode.com/docs/streams/reorg-handling · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring · also: https://blog.trailofbits.com/2023/08/23/the-engineers-guide-to-blockchain-finality/
- [statement] Envio documents an RPC race where logs from a reorged block and a header from the canonical block can be combined because RPC queries are not atomic. Hash checks must bind the event evidence to its actual block, rather than assume separate calls form one consistent snapshot. (low confidence) — https://docs.envio.dev/docs/HyperIndex/reorgs-support · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Solana processed inclusion is provisional: the block can belong to a dropped fork. A bot monitor should distinguish it from stronger commitment states. (high confidence) — https://www.helius.dev/blog/solana-commitment-levels · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring · also: https://solana.com/developers/cookbook/transactions/confirmation
- [statement] The Solana getSignatureStatuses method searches only its recent status cache unless searchTransactionHistory is included. A missing recent-cache result alone is insufficient evidence that an older transaction never landed; check the history scope before classifying it. (low confidence) — https://solana.com/docs/rpc/http/getSignatureStatuses · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring
- [statement] Ethereum proof-of-stake finality uses checkpoint votes representing at least two-thirds of staked ETH. Its official explanation says reverting a finalized block requires an attacker to lose at least one-third of staked ETH; this guarantee has explicit economic assumptions. (low confidence) — https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/ · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring
- [statement] QuickNode documents detecting a stream reorg from a parent-hash mismatch, walking backwards to the last matching block, and restreaming corrections. This provides a concrete model for bot ingestion: verify hash continuity and reconcile the displaced range. (low confidence) — https://www.quicknode.com/docs/streams/reorg-handling · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring
- [statement] The Offchain Labs postmortem reports temporary Ethereum finalization delays during the May 2023 incidents while end-user transactions were minimally impacted. This supports monitoring finality progress separately from transaction-processing availability. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/offchainlabs/post-mortem-report-ethereum-mainnet-finality-05-11-2023-95e271dfd8b2 · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring
- [statement] The Forest issue opened in May 2026 reported that log subscriptions omitted reorg-removed logs and hardcoded reverted state. This is historical implementation-gap evidence, not a claim about a currently installed release; verify the chosen client’s rollback notifications in an integration test. (low confidence) — https://github.com/ChainSafe/forest/issues/7096 · keywords: Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring

## Research summary — Crypto bot on-chain finality and reorg monitoring

A crypto bot monitor must distinguish provisional inclusion from chain-specific finality and detect when previously observed chain evidence changes. Solana commitment and blockhash expiry, Ethereum checkpoint finality, and OP Stack settlement stages need different treatment. Hash continuity, rollback-aware ingestion and consistent event/header evidence support reorg detection. Historical finality incidents and client issues show why transaction availability and notification assumptions need separate checks. Indexer rollback does not automatically undo external actions. These findings support explicit commitment tracking and reconciliation rather than a universal confirmation count.
